# 2 Maccabees Chapter 15 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 15 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_015_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

**Chapter Overview:** The final battle with Nicanor. The dream-vision of Onias and Jeremiah (vv. 11-16) is the book's most elaborate epiphany sequence. Nicanor's death and the display of his head and arm (vv. 28-35) echo both ancient trophy-display practice and the Goliath narrative (1 Sam 17:51-54). The author's closing apology (vv. 38-39) is one of the earliest explicit authorial self-assessments in ancient literature. The wine-water metaphor (v. 39) is a topos of Hellenistic literary theory.

**Key Decisions:**
- "Thrice-accursed wretch" vs. "three-times-cursed wretch" (v. 3): EMET/LOGOS "thrice-accursed" — more sonorous; PNEUMA "three-times-cursed" is acceptable; SOPHIA: "thrice-accursed wretch"
- "All-seeing" (v. 2): Greek *panepoptēs*: the all-seeing one — all three retain; a distinctive divine title in 2 Maccabees
- "A dream worthy of belief" (v. 11): Greek *hypnon axiopistos*: a dream worthy of credence — retain the epistemic qualifier; the author is vouching for the vision's authenticity
- Onias description (v. 12): the Greek is unusually elaborate; retain all elements as given; PNEUMA condenses
- "Jeremiah the prophet of God" (v. 14): all three agree
- "Shatter / strike down your adversaries" (v. 16): EMET "strike down," LOGOS "shatter" — Greek *paipakseis*: will smite/strike; LOGOS "shatter" is vivid and appropriate
- "Mordecai's day" (v. 36): Purim — the reference is explicit and all three retain it
- Closing apology (vv. 38-39): PNEUMA's rendering is the most natural; SOPHIA adopts a hybrid — the author's humility and the wine-water simile must both be fully preserved; do not abbreviate

---

**15:1** When Nicanor learned that Judas and his men were in the region of Samaria, he resolved to attack them with complete safety on the day of rest.

**15:2** The Jews who were compelled to follow him said, "Do not destroy so savagely and barbarously, but show respect for the day that the All-seeing has honored and made holy above all other days."

**15:3** The thrice-accursed wretch asked whether there was a sovereign in heaven who had commanded the observance of the sabbath day.

**15:4** When they replied, "It is the living Lord himself, the sovereign in heaven, who commanded the seventh day to be kept,"

**15:5** he retorted, "And I too am a sovereign on earth, and I command you to take up arms and carry out the king's orders." He did not, however, succeed in carrying out his plan.

**15:6** So Nicanor, in his utter arrogance and presumption, had resolved to erect a public monument of his victory over Judas and his men.

**15:7** But Maccabeus never ceased to trust with complete confidence that he would receive help from the Lord.

**15:8** He urged his men not to fear the attack of the Gentiles, but to keep in mind the help they had previously received from heaven and to expect the victory and aid that would come to them from the Almighty.

**15:9** Encouraging them from the law and the prophets, and reminding them also of the battles they had already won, he stirred up their eagerness.

**15:10** Having aroused their courage, he gave his orders, pointing out at the same time the treachery of the Gentiles and their violation of oaths.

**15:11** He armed each of them not so much with confidence in shields and spears as with the inspiration of brave words; and he cheered them all by recounting a dream worthy of belief, a sort of waking vision, as follows.

**15:12** He saw Onias, who had been high priest — a noble and good man, modest in bearing, gentle in manner, gracious in speech, and trained from childhood in all things belonging to excellence — standing with his hands outstretched, praying for the whole community of the Jews.

**15:13** Then in the same manner there appeared a man of distinguished grey hair and dignity, of marvelous and surpassing majesty.

**15:14** Onias spoke and said, "This is the man who loves his brethren and prays much for the people and the holy city — Jeremiah, the prophet of God."

**15:15** Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and delivered to Judas a golden sword, and as he gave it said:

**15:16** "Take this holy sword, a gift from God, with which you will shatter your adversaries."

**15:17** Encouraged by the words of Judas — admirable words, able to stir the soul to valor and make the hearts of the young strong — they resolved not to delay but to charge bravely and decide the matter by fighting, because the city, the sanctuary, and the holy vessels were in danger.

**15:18** Their concern for wives and children and for brothers and relatives was real, but their greatest and foremost concern was for the consecrated sanctuary.

**15:19** And those who were in the city were in no lesser distress, being troubled over the encounter in the open field.

**15:20** While everyone was now waiting for the coming decision, and the enemy had already drawn near, and the army was drawn up in battle order — the war animals stationed at a favorable position, the cavalry posted on the flanks —

**15:21** Maccabeus, surveying the forces before him, the variety of weapons, and the ferocity of the war animals, stretched out his hands toward heaven and called upon the Lord who works wonders, knowing that victory comes not from arms but that God grants it to whomever he judges worthy.

**15:22** He called out: "You, O Lord, sent your angel in the time of King Hezekiah of Judea, and he struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of Sennacherib.

**15:23** So now also, O Sovereign of the heavens, send a good angel before us to bring terror and trembling.

**15:24** By the might of your arm let those be struck down who come with blasphemy against your holy people." And with these words he ended.

**15:25** Nicanor and his men advanced with trumpets and battle songs.

**15:26** But Judas and his men met the enemy with invocations and prayers.

**15:27** Fighting with their hands and praying to God in their hearts, they laid low no fewer than thirty-five thousand men and were greatly gladdened by the manifestation of God.

**15:28** When the action was over and they were returning with joy, they recognized Nicanor lying dead in full armor.

**15:29** Then there was shouting and tumult, and they blessed the Sovereign Lord in their ancestral language.

**15:30** And the one who had in every way been the chief defender of his fellow citizens — who had maintained from his youth the love of his compatriots — commanded that Nicanor's head and arm, severed at the shoulder, be brought and put on display in Jerusalem.

**15:31** When he arrived there, he called his compatriots together and stationed the priests before the altar; then he sent for those who were in the citadel

**15:32** and showed them the head of the vile Nicanor and the arm of that blasphemer, which had been stretched out arrogantly against the holy house of the Almighty.

**15:33** He cut out the tongue of the impious Nicanor and said he would give it to the birds piecemeal; he then hung up the visible fruit of his madness opposite the sanctuary.

**15:34** Everyone looked toward heaven and blessed the glorious Lord, saying, "Blessed is he who has kept his own place undefiled."

**15:35** He hung Nicanor's head from the citadel — a clear and visible sign to all of the Lord's help.

**15:36** All decreed by common vote never to let this day go without celebration, but to observe the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which in Aramaic is called Adar — the day before Mordecai's day.

**15:37** Thus matters stood with Nicanor, and from that time the city has been in the possession of the Hebrews. And here I will bring my account to an end.

**15:38** If it is well composed and to the point, that is what I aimed at; if it is poor and mediocre, that was the best I could do.

**15:39** For just as it is harmful to drink wine by itself, or to drink only water, while wine mixed with water is both pleasant and delightful, so a well-crafted style delights the ears of those who read the composition. And with this let it end.
